title: The Water Arrives Later
logline: A famous waterfall on a highland river now falls only because a gate two kilometres upstream is opened for a fixed number of hours a day, so the drop that looks like the most self-evident thing in the landscape is in fact the last step of a chain that began somewhere else, minutes earlier.
human_question: When something answers you, where did the answer actually begin?

place.what_kind_of_place: A highland river coming off the central escarpment, and the two kilometres of it that matter: a dam and intake built across the river where the valley narrows, a long two-tier waterfall below, and between them a reach of bare rock that is wet or dry depending entirely on what is happening at the gate. Most of the river no longer goes over the fall at all. It goes into a tunnel driven for more than twelve kilometres through the hillside to an underground power station far down the same valley, which puts the water back into the same river well below the fall; and what does go over the edge is a release made under an obligation written into a regulation, a fixed volume of water run for a fixed number of daylight hours, between sunrise and sunset.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Because the most beautiful thing in the frame is also the most misleading one, and the film can prove it inside a single shot. A big two-tier fall in a gorge looks like the one thing in a landscape that is simply itself, unarguable, older than anybody. It is now an output. It starts, it runs, it thins and it stops, and none of that is decided at the fall. From the air the whole arrangement can be held in one frame: a pond behind a gate, a wet rock face, a dry rock face, and the line of the ridge under which the rest of the water is travelling in the dark towards a machine hall thirteen kilometres down the valley.
place.what_moves_or_changes: The release, which has a clock in it: the fall runs through the daylight hours and is not the same thing outside them. The weather, which fills or does not fill the reservoir and decides how much there is to divide. The season, since in heavy rain the structure spills and the argument the film is making is briefly suspended, and in drought the fall thins to a stain on the rock. And the delay itself, which is the film's subject: the interval between a gate moving and the water reaching the lip, and the far longer interval before the water that did not go over the lip does its work in the other valley.
place.when_it_looks_best: The first hour of a clear morning, when the release has begun and low sun is across the gorge, so the falling water and the dry rock beside it are both legible. The end of the day is the other shot: the same frame as the run ends. The dry months make the argument visible; the wet months make the fall look like itself again and are worth filming for exactly that contrast.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A landscape film about a great waterfall and the engineering that has quietly taken it over. Mist, black rock, a huge drop, a dam, a tunnel mouth, a river that is in two places at once, and the plain visual fact of a famous thing in the country now running to a timetable. Nothing in it needs explaining. Anyone who likes water and mountains has a whole piece, with a small shock in the middle of it.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same footage becomes the sources' own claim about what any act is made of. They say that nothing a person does, not seeing properly, not hearing, not understanding a word spoken to them, not so much as moving a hand, happens in a single moment; each of these requires a whole series, and each moment in the series does exactly one job and then hands on. That is unfilmable in a mind and perfectly filmable in this gorge, where the chain is two kilometres long and the interval between the cause and the answer is measured in minutes.

sequence.on_screen: The fall in full flow from the opposite side of the gorge, wide and high, water in two tiers, spray drifting. A long, unhurried, completely conventional shot of a great waterfall.
sequence.voice: This is the least complicated thing in the landscape. Water finds an edge and goes over it. Nobody has to be involved.

sequence.on_screen: Cut two kilometres upstream: a concrete gate structure across the narrows, the reservoir behind it flat and dark, an intake mouth, and beneath the structure a wide expanse of bare, dry rock in the riverbed.
sequence.voice: Except that it does. Most of this river now turns off here, into a tunnel more than twelve kilometres long, and comes out at a machine hall far down the same valley, which hands it back to the river well below us. What goes over the edge downstream is a release, made for a set number of hours a day, between sunrise and sunset.

sequence.on_screen: The gate at the start of a run. Machinery, a needle moving, water beginning to pass. Then the dry reach below, filmed at walking pace as the water comes down it: a tongue advancing over dry stone, filling hollows, darkening the rock.
sequence.voice: The old manuals make a claim that sounds pedantic until you watch it happen in a riverbed. Nothing anybody does, they say, takes place in one moment. Seeing properly, hearing, understanding what someone has just said to you, moving a limb, handing something over: every one of them needs a whole run of separate moments to complete [C038-M:L3; C038-M:L5].

sequence.on_screen: The lip of the fall, from directly above, in the minutes before and after the water arrives: the rock lip dark and empty, then wet, then carrying the whole flow.
sequence.voice: And each moment in the run does one job only. The books count fourteen jobs a moment of mind can do, and they are firm that a moment does one of them and hands on [C034-P:L25; C034-M:L7]. Nothing in a chain like this does two things at once, and nothing in it is in charge of the rest.

sequence.on_screen: The same wide shot of the fall as at the opening, now understood differently. Then the lower valley: the transmission line leaving the hill, a switchyard, a road, an ordinary lit house at dusk.
sequence.voice: The water that did not come over the edge is under the mountain while you watch this, in the dark, doing nothing that can be seen, and it will arrive as something else entirely and much later. One river, two answers, two different delays.

sequence.on_screen: Detail: a gauge board in the riverbed, a staff gauge at the intake, a logged reading, a clock. No faces; instruments and water.
sequence.voice: The manuals are honest about the limit here. They say the mind cannot be examined the way a river can, because it is the instrument doing the examining, and that even careful students know these sequences only by working backwards from what they can see [C038-M:L3]. This gorge is not a picture of a mind. It is the one thing a camera can do instead: a process that looks instantaneous, slowed down until its stages are two kilometres apart.

sequence.on_screen: End of the run. The flow at the lip thinning, the fall narrowing to threads, then the rock face wet but silent. Light going off the gorge.
sequence.voice: There is a further step the books insist on, which is that a name and a meaning are added after the event rather than during it [C046-P:L117-L151]. A waterfall is a name. What was here a little while ago was a release, and before that a reading, and before that rain, and none of those steps is the waterfall, and the waterfall is not any of them.

sequence.on_screen: Dawn the next day, very high. The reservoir, the gate, the dry reach, the fall not yet running, the whole arrangement in one frame in flat early light.
sequence.voice: In a few minutes this will start again, in the same order, and it will look, from the road, like water finding an edge.

concept_merge.why_together: C038 supplies the claim and this film's whole spine: nothing a person does happens in a single mind-moment, and seeing, hearing, understanding another person's words, moving a limb, giving and taking each require a whole series [C038-M:L3; C038-M:L5]. It also supplies the honesty the film needs, that the mind cannot be examined directly because it is the instrument doing the examining, so these sequences are known by inference rather than by observation [C038-M:L3]. C034 supplies the grain inside the claim: fourteen jobs, one to a moment, handed on in order [C034-P:L25; C034-M:L7], which is what turns a vague chain into an arrangement with stages. C046 supplies the last and most useful step, that the name and the meaning of a thing arrive after the event, in separate later processes [C046-P:L117-L151], which is exactly what happens when a scheduled release is seen from the road and called a waterfall.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the feeling of immediacy is a feature of the ending of a process rather than evidence about its length. C038 alone is an assertion no camera can test. C034 alone is a list. C046 alone is a point about naming. Together, on two kilometres of river where the stages have been pulled physically apart and given clocks, they let a viewer watch a thing that looks self-evident turn out to be the last step of something that began elsewhere, without any person in the frame being offered as the one doing it.

concept_links.why: The digest's central report is the Margaya's flat claim that nothing a person does happens in a single mind-moment, and that properly seeing, hearing, understanding someone's words, moving a limb, giving and taking each need a whole series [C038-M:L3; C038-M:L5]; the Pradeepika then supplies the six sixes by which any moment in a process is located and the division into five-door and mind-door processes. The film is built on the first of those and on the digest's frankest passage, that the mind is the hardest thing to study because it is the very tool doing the studying, so even students know the processes only by inference [C038-M:L3]. That sentence is spoken in the sixth beat, because it is the only honest answer to the obvious objection that a gorge is not a mind. The digest's limits are carried exactly. The film never suggests that slowing down will let anyone watch their own moments arise, since the source says people do not notice these processes at all. It does not present the series as information processing or as a stream of consciousness. And it does not put the group's framing, that there is no separate seer behind the seeing, into this concept's mouth: the digest states plainly that the extracts do not make that claim, so the narration here keeps to what the source does say, which is that an act is a series of hand-offs with no step that performs the whole act.

The digest gives the fourteen functions and the rule the film's fourth beat depends on, that every mind-moment does exactly one job and that a mind does only one job at a time [C034-P:L25; C034-M:L7]; the digest's own image for it is a relay rather than a watcher. That is what a gate, a reach of rock, a lip and a tunnel are: stages that cannot do each other's work. The digest's limits are honoured. This is not offered as a technique for watching each step, since the source says countless moments pass in a finger-snap. The background current is not described as a subconscious or a hidden self, and it is not narrated here at all. The impulsion stage is never presented as a conscious pause in which options are weighed, and the popular slogan about a gap between stimulus and response is deliberately avoided even though this film is about an interval, because the digest says the slogan borrows the shape and adds a claim the source does not make. The source's link between weak rebirth-producing action and being born blind or deaf [C034-P:L47] is not narrated and is not carried into any judgement about any person.

The digest's account of the four mind-door processes that follow a single sight, taking the object as past, then its colour, then its name or concept, then its meaning, with a full wholesome or unwholesome response possible only in the last [C046-P:L117-L151], is what the closing beat uses: the word waterfall arrives after the event it names, and arrives at whoever is standing on the road rather than at the river. The digest's limits are kept. Naming is not treated as an error to be given up, because the source treats it as an ordinary step in knowing. No popular figures for recognition speed are offered as corroboration. The mind door is used only in its technical sense as a particular mind-moment [C046-P:L39], never as a metaphor for openness. And the registration step, which the digest notes takes only sense-sphere objects [C046-M:L52-L54], is not stretched into a claim about lingering impressions of scenery.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That the immediacy of an experience is not evidence that it happened all at once. Something can feel like a single unarguable fact and still be the last stage of an ordered series that started elsewhere and took time to arrive; and the name we give the whole thing attaches to the end of the chain, not to any of the steps that made it.
what_must_be_real: The scheme, the schedule and the loss. The reduction of the fall is a real change to a real river with consequences for the people, water users and habitat below it, and the film may not treat it as a clever visual conceit; what is said about volumes, hours and obligations must be what the operator and the record actually say, not what makes a better sentence. Nothing is released, held back or timed for the camera, and no request is made to alter a run. No operator, engineer or gatekeeper is filmed as the one who decides, or cut so that a person becomes the mind in the analogy; the stages are the subject. If the fall cannot be filmed safely from the gorge side, it is not filmed from there.
position_hint: middle: it is the group's clearest demonstration that a single apparent act is a series with intervals in it, so it works best after the opening film about what arrives at the senses and before the films about how fast a response is formed. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Presenting the gorge as a picture of a mind. The C038 digest is explicit that the mind cannot be watched directly and is known only by inference; the film must say so rather than let the analogy pass as evidence.
Sliding into the slogan about a gap between stimulus and response where freedom lies. The C034 digest names this as a borrowed shape that adds a claim the source does not make.
Suggesting that anyone can slow down and observe their own mind-moments, which both digests rule out.

Letting the film become an advocacy piece for or against the diversion, or making claims about flows, obligations or damage that the operator and the record would not support. The dispute behind this scheme is long, dated and documented on both sides, and the film records it without taking a side or supplying a villain.

Lament. A film that mourns a diminished waterfall is doing the one thing the concepts here do not do; C061's bar on legacy and remembrance framing applies to a landscape as much as to a person. The earlier size of the fall belongs in the film as a dated photograph, not as a loss to be felt.

Framing any worker at the headworks as the decider, or building the chain around a person so that the film supplies the single doer the concepts deny. The release is run through a valve on a schedule set in a regulation; no operator is the mind in the analogy.

Quoting a single figure for the release as though the record agreed. It does not: the same volume is reported both as a continuous flow for ten and a half hours and as ten half-hour periods, and the obligation is expressed as conditional on the natural flow being there.
Carrying the source's link between weak past action and being born blind or deaf into the film in any form [C034-P:L47].

Becoming a tea-country film by default. The surrounding slopes are planted, and the series already has films in that landscape; the framing must stay on the river, the rock and the structure. The estate that gave the fall its name is a fact for the research block, not a subject for the camera.

Becoming a second film about the consequences of a hydro scheme. The slate already has one on this river system, and this film's subject is a thing that happens only when water is released, not a thing revealed when water is taken away.
drop_if: The release schedule turns out not to be observable, or the fall runs the same way whatever the gate does, which would remove the film's only argument.

The release is not in fact run, so that the fall simply follows the weather; the regulation makes the flow compulsory only so far as the natural flow of the river supplies it, and in a dry enough year there may be nothing to schedule.
Neither the headworks nor the gorge can be filmed, or drone clearance over the dam and the reserve is refused.
It could only be made by asking for a release to be started, stopped or altered for the camera.

connections.note: Two ways of getting at something too fast to watch: one slows a rhythm into spoken syllables, the other finds a process whose stages are already two kilometres apart.
One film is about a response so fast that nobody can find a decision inside it; this one is about a response whose steps have been pulled far enough apart to be timed.

Both films stand on the same river system and both have an engineering scheme in their history, and that is the whole of the overlap. The other film is about a building that is always there and becomes visible when water is taken away; its engine is a level falling. This one is about an event that does not exist unless water is let out, on a clock, and its engine is a release arriving. The other film's material - a valley filled, settlements moved, a drowned building coming back - is not part of this one: submergence, displacement and loss are outside this film's subject entirely, and the two must not be shot, cut or narrated as a pair. If either film starts to need the other's history to make its point, one of them is wrong.

Research on 2026-09-26 found that both films now sit on released water: the run of rapids in that film lost most of its natural flow to a run-of-river diversion and is sustained by a daytime release agreed after objection, exactly as this fall is. The two must not converge. Here the release is the subject — a gazetted volume, a valve built to produce a waterfall, and a daylight window that exists because of when people look. There it is background, and the subject is the point on smooth water past which nothing can be reconsidered. This film owns the schedule; that one never argues from it.

selection.reason: It is the only place found where a chain that normally feels instantaneous has been physically stretched out, given a clock, and left visible in one aerial frame.

review.note: Rewritten 2026-09-22 into the footage-led shape. The old subject, an interpreter followed through the pause between hearing and speaking, is dropped: it made one person the assembler of an understanding, which is what these concepts deny, and the pause itself is unfilmable. The concept is kept and moved to a place where the gap between receiving and responding is structural, scheduled and visible from the air. A railway token exchange was considered and rejected because the slate already carries two railway films. Concepts re-read from the digests as a new reader; every citation re-verified against digest evidence; the earlier merged-into relation with IDEA-0085 is replaced by a pairing, since this is again a standalone film. Researched properly on 2026-09-26 and a historical_thread added; the verdict stays pending because it was never given, not because the body was rewritten again. The research corrected one thing the earlier draft had wrong and it touches the prose: the diverted water does not go to a power station in another valley. The tunnel runs down this same valley and the station returns the water to the same river a short distance above the older reservoir downstream, so two sequence lines, two place lines and one shot in what_to_film were changed to say that. One invented figure was also removed from the closing beat, which had the release arriving twenty minutes earlier; nothing found documents the travel time from gate to lip and it is now an unknown rather than a number in the voice. The argument, the two layers, the beat order and the concept merge are unchanged.

suggested_location.name: St Clair's Falls and the Upper Kotmale headworks on the Kotmale Oya at Talawakele

also_known_as.name: Maha Ella
also_known_as.meaning: the great fall; the main drop, given as about 80 m high and about 50 m wide
also_known_as.used_by: Sri Lankan usage, in guides and local description

also_known_as.name: Kuda Ella
also_known_as.meaning: the small fall; the second, lesser drop of about 50 m, which some accounts place upstream of the main fall and others downstream

also_known_as.name: the little Niagara of Sri Lanka
also_known_as.meaning: the tourist name the fall has carried for a century, earned by its width rather than its height

suggested_location.region: Nuwara Eliya District, Central Province: the Kotmale Oya where it comes off the escarpment near Talawakele, between Hatton and Nuwara Eliya
suggested_location.why_here: It is the only site found where the film's argument is also its most beautiful shot, and where that argument is a dated document rather than a resemblance. A large two-tier fall sits a little over two kilometres below a run-of-river intake dam whose headrace tunnel, the longest in the country, takes most of the river more than twelve kilometres down the same valley to an underground power station and returns it to the river far below the fall. What still goes over the lip is there because a regulation says it must be: the National Environmental (Upper Kotmale Hydro-Power Project - Monitoring) Regulations, No. 1 of 2003, published in Gazette Extraordinary No. 1283/19 of 10 April 2003, fix a volume of 47,250 cubic metres for this fall within a window between sunrise and sunset, and one of the technical committees that rejected the project earlier had asked in so many words that the waterfalls stay in their natural condition at least during the day time. So the release exists because of when people look at it. The stages of a process that would elsewhere be instantaneous are laid out along two kilometres of river with a clock and a valve attached - and the valve is documented: a dissertation was written on automating it - while an aerial can hold pond, gate, dry reach and falling water in one frame. Photographs of the fall from before the scheme and after it are published and dated, which gives the film its comparison without staging anything.

historical_thread.story:
The Kotmale Oya, one of the largest tributaries of the Mahaweli Ganga, comes off the western slopes of the Nuwara Eliya range between about 700 and 1,200 m above sea level. Roughly three kilometres west of the valley town of Talawakele it goes over three rock outcrops in two falls: the greater, Maha Ella, usually given as 80 m high and about 50 m wide, and a lesser one, Kuda Ella, given as 50 m. The name on the map is not the river's. It belongs to the St. Clair tea estate the river runs through, planted in the 1870s, and the falls have carried the estate's name ever since; guidebooks have called them the little Niagara of Sri Lanka on the strength of the width rather than the height. Wikipedia ranks them the twentieth highest waterfall in the country while Sri Lankan sources call them the widest. Devon Falls, 97 m high and six kilometres west, is named the same way, after an English coffee planter called Devon whose plantation was nearby. Both stand beside a main highway of the central hills, which is part of why they matter to this story: an official paper notes that at least five world-class waterfalls lie in the project area and that, unlike others, they are easily reached by anyone on public transport.

The state's interest in this stretch of river begins with the 1968 Master Plan for Mahaweli development prepared by the United Nations Development Programme and the Food and Agriculture Organization. In 1980 a joint Ceylon Electricity Board and German Technical Cooperation team proposed a cascade of stations of 64 to 93 MW here as part of a master plan for electricity supply. A feasibility study funded by Japan ran from 1985 to 1987, and a team of Japanese consultants formulated the project that followed; the study was not public until 1992. In 1992 the Ceylon Electricity Board decided to proceed and sought a Japanese loan for detailed design and an environmental impact assessment. The scheme was originally proposed at 248 MW and cut to 150 MW, to contribute 530 GWh a year. As formulated it was to harness seven tributaries - Devon Oya, St. Andrews Stream, Pundal Oya, Puna Oya, Ramboda Oya, St. Clair's and Holyrood - by taking water above several waterfalls. An earlier candidate dam site at Caledonia was dropped because it would have displaced more than 2,700 families, and Talawakele was chosen instead.

What followed is a dispute with dates on it. The environmental impact assessment report was submitted in 1994 - September in the account by the Environmental Foundation Limited's own staff, December in other accounts - with the Ministry of Irrigation, Power and Highways as project approving agency and the Ceylon Electricity Board as proponent. Its Technical Evaluation Committee issued a report rejecting the project on 7 February 1995. An oversight committee appointed over that committee recommended approval on 25 February 1995, and the Central Environmental Authority refused the concurrence the approval needed, nullifying it. The Board appealed on 23 March 1995 under section 23DD(1) of the National Environmental Act, No. 47 of 1980; a panel of experts heard the appeal with public participation and endorsed the refusal on 30 June 1995, and on 3 August 1995 the Secretary to the Ministry of Transport, Environment and Women's Affairs dismissed the appeal, criticising the approving agency for recommending approval when its own committee had rejected the project. In September 1996 the Board issued an addendum on the alternative Yoxford site, arguing it was neither feasible nor economical; a committee appointed by the Central Environmental Authority rejected the addendum in December 1996 and asked for core drilling at that site. The Board appealed again on 2 April 1997. Conditional approval was granted by the Secretary to the Ministry of Forestry and Environment in 1998 - the dates given are 2 July 1998, a decision quoted as of 16 July 1998, and August 1998 - after a hearing at which no member of the public was present. The Environmental Foundation Limited filed a writ application in the Court of Appeal seeking a stay order and a fair hearing, on the ground that its exclusion from the second appeal was arbitrary and contrary to the Central Environmental Authority's own public participation handbook, and that rejecting one alternative was not a consideration of alternatives. The case ended in a settlement under which the state agreed to hold a fresh appeal with the Foundation taking part. That hearing began on 22 October 1999 and approval followed on 27 March 2000, with mitigatory measures attached. An Inter-Ministerial Committee reported on the project in July 2002 and a parliamentary sub-committee was still sitting in 2004.

The grounds of objection were specific. No serious evaluation of alternatives: the Yoxford option, proposed on environmental grounds by the Central Engineering Consultancy Bureau - a government engineering firm and a partner in the feasibility group - is put at 120 MW and 370 GWh in one account and 100 MW in another, with about eleven kilometres of tunnel, no resettlement and no waterfall destroyed. The destruction of St. Clair major, St. Clair minor and Devon and reduced flow at Ramboda, Puna and Pundal. Landslide-prone ground: the whole valley is classified as landslide-prone, the rock is highly fractured charnockitic gneiss under thick colluvium, and a crystalline limestone band runs through the area - the same feature on which the Yoxford alternative was rejected. The drying of a long downstream stretch of river and its consequences for water users and for fauna and flora. Heavy erosion. An inadequate relocation plan. And valuation: the approving agency's own committee found the weight given to the waterfalls inadequate, no economic value assigned to them, and recommended a contingent valuation exercise, adding that the waterfalls should remain in their natural condition at least during the day time. The objectors were not one campaign. They included the Central Environmental Authority, which refused twice; three technical committees; the Environmental Foundation Limited, which litigated; Hemantha Withanage, who put the case to the World Commission on Dams' South Asia regional consultation under the title 'Upper Kotmale Hydropower Project: Another Disaster in Dam History'; the People's Campaign Against Upper Kotmale Project; the then Minister of Housing and Plantation Infrastructure, who was also general secretary of the Ceylon Workers' Congress, whose members predominate among the inhabitants of the project area; an Inter-Ministerial Committee; and a parliamentary sub-committee. The same record is read two ways by the same organisation at different times. A 2004 paper by Dekshika Charmini Kodituwakku and Vinod Moonesinghe of the Environmental Foundation Limited concludes that the assessment report was seriously flawed and that alternatives were 'rejected almost offhandedly'. A 2021 Foundation blog post by Anjalee Udawatta and Lakshitha Edirisinghe reads the same sequence of rejections, appeals and conditions as a case in which public participation and the assessment process ultimately balanced development against protection.

The mitigation is where the waterfall acquires a timetable. The settlement produced a monitoring committee chaired by the Central Environmental Authority with a seat for the Environmental Foundation Limited, and the Board was required to gauge the stream flow of the five affected falls - Devon, St. Clair's, Puna Oya, Ramboda and Dunsinane - to prepare a watershed management plan, assess biodiversity, monitor the water table, plan landslide mitigation, dispose of tunnel muck, and maintain a complete standardised photographic record of the waterfalls from the date the project began. These became the National Environmental (Upper Kotmale Hydro-Power Project - Monitoring) Regulations, No. 1 of 2003, made by the minister in charge of the environment under paragraph (r) of subsection (2) of section 32 of the National Environmental Act No. 47 of 1980 and published in Gazette Extraordinary No. 1283/19 of 10 April 2003. The Foundation's seat on the monitoring committee is section 4(w); Schedule II holds the mitigation measures; the Ministry of Irrigation and Water Management was made responsible for seeing that the measures affecting the waterfalls' aesthetic value were carried out.

The numbers in that regulation are the heart of this film, and the sources do not agree on them. For Devon Falls, a total volume of 18,000 cubic metres of water a day, released for a minimum of ten hours daily between sunrise and sunset, provided that such quantity is available from the natural flow of the stream. For St. Clair's, a total volume of 47,250 cubic metres. On the schedule, the widely repeated version - encyclopaedic, governmental and touristic alike - is a continuous flow of 47,250 cubic metres over the falls for 10 hours and 30 minutes daily, between sunrise and sunset. The Foundation's own 2004 paper, citing the gazette directly, writes instead of 47,250 cubic metres per day 'for ten half hour periods'. Those are not the same instruction. A continuous ten and a half hours works out at about 1.25 cubic metres a second; ten half-hour periods would be the same volume delivered in ten separate runs at five times the rate.

In 2005 the Cabinet approved the project with significant modifications, curtailing the diversions so as to reduce the effect on the waterfalls: water was no longer to be taken from any of them except St. Clair's. Construction began in 2005 or 2006 and the project was commissioned on 14 July 2012. What was built is a single concrete gravity intake dam across the Kotmale Oya just below Talawakele - 34 m high in the design paper, 35.5 m high with a 180 m crest in the official description - impounding a pond of 2.5 million cubic metres gross and 0.8 million effective at a full supply level of 1,194 m: a run-of-river arrangement rather than a storage reservoir, with spillway gates that open automatically in heavy rain. From it a headrace tunnel of 12.5 to 12.89 km, the longest excavated tunnel in the country, and a 796 m penstock drop a gross head of 491 m to an underground power house at Niyamgamdora, about two kilometres upstream of the confluence with the Puna Oya and about two kilometres above the older Kotmale reservoir, holding two vertical Francis units - 75 MW each officially, 77 MW each in the design paper - for 150 MW installed and 409 GWh a year. A tailrace tunnel of 0.46 km returns the water to the same river. Cost is given as Rs. 37,269 million by the energy ministry and Rs. 44 billion by Wikipedia, with the Japanese loan put at ¥33.265 billion or US$ 251 million, signed in 2002. The number of households moved is given as 470, 495, 524 and 538 in different accounts, and one survey before construction counted 538 houses in the low-lying parts of the town that would need resettlement or relocation.

One further piece of engineering is on the record, and it is the most useful single fact here. During construction a special valve was to be installed near the dam's bottom outlet for the sole purpose of releasing water to maintain the waterfall. In 2006 R. A. L. Ranawake submitted an MEng dissertation in the Department of Electrical Engineering at the University of Moratuwa, supervised by L. Udawatta, titled 'Waterfall maintenance of the upper Kotmale hydropower project', whose stated object was 'to develop an automated system for the optimum water release from the reservoir while meeting the conditions specified in the gazette'. A program was written to automate the operation of that valve, and a graphical user interface was built to let an operator communicate with the controlling system. The falls, in other words, were turned into a control problem and solved as one.

Since commissioning, the fall runs and is widely reported to be much reduced; Sri Lankan travel and encyclopaedic writing says the water has dwindled so far that it has lost its glory. Lists of the affected waterfalls carry percentage figures - a 70 per cent reduction at Puna Oya Ella, 50 per cent at Ramboda Ella, and St. Andrews, 50 m, expected to disappear altogether - but those describe the scheme as proposed rather than as built, since the 2005 modification dropped those diversions. The dam spills when the catchment is wet: a photograph dated 2 August 2012 shows all five spillway gates open, and on the morning of 3 August 2026 three gates opened automatically after heavy rain over the catchment, with the Disaster Management Centre noting increased flow at both St. Clair's and Devon Falls.
historical_thread.how_it_binds:
The film's existing claim is that the most self-evident thing in view is the last step of a sequence that started elsewhere. The history makes that literal, and it dates it. C038's central report is the Margaya's flat statement that nothing a person does happens in a single mind-moment: seeing properly, hearing, understanding what someone has just said, moving a limb, giving and taking each require a whole series [C038-M:L3; C038-M:L5]. That is a claim about mind and no camera can test it. What this place supplies is the same shape in a form that can be filmed and, more than that, read: a landmark named after a tea estate in the 1870s, photographed for a century, ranked in lists of the country's waterfalls, is now an output of a schedule, and there is a document with a number on it - Gazette Extraordinary No. 1283/19 of 10 April 2003 - specifying the volume and the daylight window within which the waterfall is to exist.

C034 supplies the grain, and the built scheme has it exactly. The digest's rule is that every mind-moment does one job and hands on, and that a mind does only one job at a time [C034-P:L25; C034-M:L7]; its own image for this is a relay rather than a watcher. The chain here is a relay in which no stage can do another's work, and half of it is administrative rather than physical: rain over a catchment, an inflow, a pond of two and a half million cubic metres that cannot store a season, a gauged flow, a condition in a schedule, a valve at a bottom outlet, a program operating that valve, an interface where an operator sees it happen, a reach of dry rock, a lip. Not one of those stages is the waterfall, and the waterfall is not any of them. The 2006 dissertation is the plainest statement of this the record offers: the existence of a famous waterfall during daylight hours was treated as a control problem and solved with software. That is the relay made institutional.

C046 is where this location stops being a good illustration and becomes the right one. The digest's account of the four mind-door processes after a single sight - the object taken as past, then its colour, then its name or concept, then its meaning, with a full wholesome or unwholesome response possible only in the last [C046-P:L117-L151] - says that the name and the meaning arrive after the event they belong to. The regulation was written in that order. The technical committee's finding was that the waterfalls should remain in their natural condition at least during the day time, and that no economic value had been assigned to them, and that a contingent valuation should be done: which is to say that the flow was scheduled for the hours in which it would be looked at, and priced by asking people what the looking was worth. The release is timed to the viewer, not to the river. And the same set of conditions requires a complete standardised photographic record of the waterfalls from the date the project began - a record of the thing, made by rule, after the fact. The word 'waterfall' arrives at whoever is standing on the road; so, now, does the water.

The limits matter as much as the fit, and the digests set them. C038's digest is explicit that the mind cannot be examined the way a river can, because it is the instrument doing the examining, and that even students know these processes only by inference [C038-M:L3]; so the gorge is never offered as a picture of a mind, and the film says so in the voice rather than letting the analogy pass as evidence. The same digest says the group's 'no separate seer' framing is not in these extracts, so the history is not used to smuggle it in: what is shown is a series of hand-offs in which no step performs the whole act. C034's digest rules out the slogan about a gap between stimulus and response even though this film is about an interval, and rules out the idea that anyone can slow down and watch their own moments. C046's digest says naming is an ordinary step in knowing and not an error, so the film does not treat the word for this place as a mistake that a purer seeing would drop, and it offers no popular figures about recognition speed as corroboration.

Two things the history is not for. It is not a verdict. A project was opposed by named bodies on named grounds over roughly a decade, rejected repeatedly, litigated, modified and approved, and the accounts of it disagree about the dates and about what the disagreement proved; the film sets that down once, keeps the variants apart, and takes no side, because nothing in these three digests licenses an opinion about a power scheme and a film that acquired one would stop being about the order of stages. Nor is it an elegy. The earlier size of the fall belongs here as a dated photograph beside a later dated photograph, which is what the concepts need - one arrangement, then another - and not as something to mourn; C061's bar on legacy and remembrance framing is why. The film is about a thing that happens when water is let out, which is a beginning, not a loss.
what_is_certain: The falls stand on the Kotmale Oya, one of the largest tributaries of the Mahaweli Ganga, about three kilometres west of Talawakele in the Nuwara Eliya district, and are named after the St. Clair tea estate the river runs through. The main fall, Maha Ella, is given as 80 m high and about 50 m wide; the lesser fall, Kuda Ella, as 50 m. The falls are commonly called the little Niagara of Sri Lanka.

Devon Falls, 97 m high, lies about six kilometres west of Talawakele and is named after an English coffee planter called Devon whose plantation was nearby. Both falls stand beside a main highway of the central hills, and the 2004 Environmental Foundation Limited paper records that at least five world-class waterfalls lie within the project area and are, unlike others, easily accessible to anyone using public transport.

The state's interest in this stretch begins with the 1968 UNDP/FAO Master Plan for Mahaweli development. In 1980 a Ceylon Electricity Board and German Technical Cooperation team proposed a cascade of stations of 64-93 MW here. A feasibility study funded by Japan ran 1985-1987 and Japanese consultants formulated the project; the study was not public until 1992. In 1992 the Board decided to proceed and sought a Japanese loan for detailed design and an EIA.

The project was originally proposed at 248 MW and reduced to 150 MW, to contribute 530 GWh a year. As formulated it was to harness seven tributaries - Devon Oya, St. Andrews Stream, Pundal Oya, Puna Oya, Ramboda Oya, St. Clair's and Holyrood - by diverting water above several waterfalls. An earlier candidate site at Caledonia was dropped because it would have displaced over 2,700 families, and Talawakele was chosen instead.

The EIA was rejected repeatedly. A Technical Evaluation Committee report rejecting the project is dated 7 February 1995; an oversight committee recommended approval on 25 February 1995 and the Central Environmental Authority refused the concurrence that approval required; the Board appealed on 23 March 1995 under section 23DD(1) of the National Environmental Act No. 47 of 1980; a panel of experts endorsed the refusal on 30 June 1995; and on 3 August 1995 the Secretary to the Ministry of Transport, Environment and Women's Affairs dismissed the appeal, criticising the approving agency for recommending approval against its own committee's finding.

In September 1996 the Board submitted an addendum on the alternative Yoxford site claiming it was neither feasible nor economical; a committee appointed by the Central Environmental Authority rejected the addendum in December 1996 and recommended core drilling at that site. The Board appealed again on 2 April 1997.

Conditional approval was granted in 1998 by the Secretary to the Ministry of Forestry and Environment after a hearing at which no member of the public was present. The Environmental Foundation Limited filed a writ application in the Court of Appeal seeking a stay order and a fair hearing; the case was settled on terms that a fresh appeal be held with the Foundation participating. That appeal hearing began on 22 October 1999 and approval with mitigatory measures followed on 27 March 2000. An Inter-Ministerial Committee reported in July 2002; a parliamentary sub-committee was still sitting in 2004.

The grounds of objection recorded in the Withanage paper and the Kodituwakku and Moonesinghe paper include: failure to identify or evaluate suitable alternatives; destruction of St. Clair major, St. Clair minor and Devon falls and reduced flow at Ramboda, Puna and Pundal; landslide-prone geology, fractured charnockitic gneiss, thick colluvium and a crystalline limestone band; drying of a long downstream stretch of river with consequences for water users and for fauna and flora; heavy erosion; an inadequate relocation plan; and inadequate weight and no economic valuation given to the waterfalls.

The Yoxford alternative was proposed on environmental grounds by the Central Engineering Consultancy Bureau, a government engineering firm and a partner in the feasibility group. It involved about eleven kilometres of tunnel, no resettlement and the destruction of no waterfall. It was rejected on geological grounds - a crystalline limestone band and landslide danger - which the 2004 paper notes are present at the chosen site as well.

The approving agency's own Technical Evaluation Committee found that the weight given to the waterfalls in the EIA was inadequate, that no economic values had been assigned to them, that a contingent valuation exercise should be conducted, and that the waterfalls should remain in their natural condition at least during the day time.

The objectors were multiple and institutional: the Central Environmental Authority, three technical committees, the Environmental Foundation Limited, Hemantha Withanage at the World Commission on Dams South Asia regional consultation, the People's Campaign Against Upper Kotmale Project, the then Minister of Housing and Plantation Infrastructure who was also general secretary of the Ceylon Workers' Congress, an Inter-Ministerial Committee and a parliamentary sub-committee.

The settlement produced a monitoring committee chaired by the Central Environmental Authority with a seat for the Environmental Foundation Limited. The Board was required to gauge the stream flow of the five affected falls - Devon, St. Clair's, Puna Oya, Ramboda and Dunsinane - prepare a watershed management plan, assess biodiversity, monitor the water table, plan landslide mitigation, dispose of tunnel muck, and maintain a complete standardised photographic record of the waterfalls from the date the project began.

These conditions were made law as the National Environmental (Upper Kotmale Hydro-Power Project - Monitoring) Regulations, No. 1 of 2003, made under paragraph (r) of subsection (2) of section 32 of the National Environmental Act No. 47 of 1980 and published in Gazette Extraordinary No. 1283/19 of 10 April 2003. The Foundation's seat on the monitoring committee is section 4(w); Schedule II contains the mitigation measures; the Ministry of Irrigation and Water Management was designated to ensure that the measures protecting the waterfalls' aesthetic value were implemented.

The release for this fall is a gazetted obligation, not an informal practice, and the figure for it is 47,250 cubic metres. For Devon Falls the figure is a total of 18,000 cubic metres a day released for a minimum of ten hours daily between sunrise and sunset, expressed as conditional on that quantity being available from the natural flow of the stream. Devon Falls is therefore the one other waterfall found anywhere in the country under a comparable written release obligation, and it is under the same regulation.

In 2005 the Cabinet approved the project with modifications curtailing the diversions, so that water was no longer to be taken from any of the affected waterfalls except St. Clair's. Construction followed and the project was commissioned on 14 July 2012.

The built scheme is a single run-of-river concrete gravity intake dam across the Kotmale Oya below Talawakele, with spillway gates that open automatically in heavy rain; a headrace tunnel described as the longest excavated tunnel in Sri Lanka; a 796 m penstock; a gross head of 491 m; an underground power house at Niyamgamdora about two kilometres upstream of the confluence with the Puna Oya and about two kilometres above the older Kotmale reservoir; two vertical Francis units for 150 MW installed and 409 GWh a year; and a tailrace tunnel of 0.46 km returning the water to the same river. The energy ministry gives the pond a full supply level of 1,194 m above mean sea level, gross storage 2.5 million cubic metres and effective storage 0.8 million.
The Japanese loan was signed in 2002 and is given as ¥33.265 billion or US$ 251 million.

A special valve was to be installed near the dam's bottom outlet for the purpose of releasing water to maintain the waterfall. R. A. L. Ranawake's 2006 MEng dissertation in the Department of Electrical Engineering at the University of Moratuwa, supervised by L. Udawatta, 'Waterfall maintenance of the upper Kotmale hydropower project', states its object as developing an automated system for the optimum water release from the reservoir while meeting the conditions specified in the gazette, and reports a program written to automate the operation of that valve and a graphical user interface built to let an operator communicate with the controlling system.

The dam spills when the catchment is wet. A photograph dated 2 August 2012 shows all five spillway gates open. Ada Derana reported that three spill gates opened automatically on the morning of 3 August 2026 after heavy rain in the catchment, and that the Disaster Management Centre noted increased water flow at St. Clair's and Devon Falls.

Photographs of the fall exist from before and after the scheme and are dated: Wikimedia Commons holds images with camera dates of 6 September 2008 and 23 April 2011, both before commissioning, and of 21 September 2015 and 6 February 2026 after it. The Wikipedia article uses a 2008 and a 2018 photograph side by side to show the reduction.
what_is_disputed: The release schedule itself, which is the film's central production fact. The widely repeated version - Wikipedia, Sri Lankan reference sites, tourism pages - is a continuous flow of 47,250 cubic metres over the falls for 10 hours and 30 minutes daily, between sunrise and sunset. The 2004 Environmental Foundation Limited paper, citing the gazette directly, writes instead of 47,250 cubic metres per day 'for ten half hour periods'. The volume agrees; the delivery does not, and they imply different films. The gazette itself was not read for this record.

Whether the obligation is conditional. The Devon Falls condition as quoted carries a proviso that the quantity be available from the natural flow of the stream. Whether the same proviso attaches to this fall was not established, though it would explain both the reported dwindling of the flow and the pond's inability to store water for a dry spell.

Whether the release is in fact run as gazetted today. The regulation and the valve are documented; compliance is not. Travel and reference writing says the water has dwindled so far that the fall has lost its glory, and no monitoring report, gauge record or photographic series was located.
The date the EIA report was submitted: September 1994 in the Kodituwakku and Moonesinghe paper, December 1994 in the Withanage paper and in later summaries.

The date and author of the decisive approval. 2 July 1998 and a decision quoted as of 16 July 1998 appear in the 2004 paper's own chronology; August 1998 appears in the Withanage paper and in the Foundation's 2021 blog; 27 March 2000 is the approval after the reopened appeal; 2002 appears in the International Rivers account as the year the Ministry of Forestry and Environment approved the project; and 2003 and 2005 both appear as the year Cabinet approved it. These are probably different milestones rather than a contradiction, but no single document reconciling them was found. The 2004 chronology is internally inconsistent as printed, giving the writ filed on 6 October 1998 and the case concluded on 17 July 1998.

How many rejections there were and by whom. 'Rejected thrice under the National Environmental Act' is the Withanage formula - twice by the Central Environmental Authority and once by the Secretary to the Ministry of Transport, Environment and Women's Affairs. The 2004 chronology counts five rejections by labelling each step. The Foundation's 2021 post says the proposal was rejected by the Authority twice.

How many waterfalls were at stake: five in the 2004 paper and in the monitoring conditions, six in the Wikipedia articles, seven in the Sri Lankan reference accounts and in the list of streams. The difference is partly between falls that were to be dewatered and falls that were to be reduced.
The capacity of the Yoxford alternative: 120 MW and 370 GWh in the 2004 paper, 100 MW in the Withanage paper, which also says that with a Lindula option the pair would generate 180 MW.

Costs. The original scheme and the Yoxford option were costed at US$ 257 million and US$ 246 million in the addendum, while the Central Engineering Consultancy Bureau's own estimate for its option was US$ 178 million; the 2004 paper says the consultants had costed a different layout. The completed project is put at Rs. 37,269 million by the energy ministry and Rs. 44 billion by Wikipedia.

Dam and tunnel dimensions. The dam is 34 m high in the 2004 design account and 35.5 m high with a 180 m crest in the official description; one summary garbles it as 34 feet. The headrace tunnel is given as 12.5 km, 12.8 km and 12.89 km. The turbines are 75 MW each officially and 77 MW each in the design account; one summary garbles them as 7 MW.

How many households were moved: 470, 495, 524 and 538 appear in different accounts, and a survey before construction counted 538 houses in the low-lying parts of the town needing resettlement or relocation.

The size and standing of the fall. 80 m for the main drop is standard; the width is given as about 50 m; the ranking is twentieth highest in the country in Wikipedia while Sri Lankan sources call it the widest in the country, and one account gives the site's elevation as 1,076.92 m. Accounts also disagree on whether the lesser fall lies upstream or downstream of the main one, and on whether the arrangement is two falls or three.

Reduction percentages in circulation - 70 per cent at Puna Oya Ella, 50 per cent at Ramboda Ella, and St. Andrews expected to disappear altogether - describe the scheme as proposed. The 2005 modification dropped those diversions, and a 2026 report notes flow at Devon Falls rising with rain over the catchment, so these figures should not be used for the built project.

Whether any tributary intakes were built at all. The 2004 design account describes tributary diversion facilities as part of the scheme; the official descriptions of the completed project name only the Talawakele intake. Nothing found settles what was constructed and abandoned.

Whether any other waterfall in the country stands in this position. Devon Falls does, under the same regulation. Laxapana Falls is reported to carry much less water than before the two Laxapana stations were built, and Aberdeen Falls stands on a diverted river, but no scheduled or gazetted release was found for either, and no national register of such obligations was located.

Earlier alteration of this fall before the scheme. Nothing was found: no earlier intake, estate diversion or mini-hydro above the falls is recorded in the sources consulted, and an absence of records is not evidence that there was none.

What none of this settles. The record establishes what was proposed, who objected, on what grounds, what was decided and when, and what volume and window were written into a regulation. It does not settle whether the project should have been built, whether the assessment process worked or failed, or what the fall was worth; the same organisation's own publications read the outcome both ways seventeen years apart, and nothing in this block is to be taken as an answer.

what_to_film: The fall in full release from the far side of the gorge, filmed conventionally and at length, so that the later revelation lands against it.
The headworks: the gate structure across the narrows, the intake mouth, the surface of the pond behind it, and the bare riverbed immediately below.
The start of a run, followed downstream: the tongue of water advancing over dry rock, filling hollows and darkening stone.
The lip of the fall from directly overhead in the minutes before, during and after the arrival of the flow.
The end of a run: the flow thinning, the threads breaking, the wet silent rock face.
One aerial that holds pond, gate, dry reach and fall together, in raking light.

The bottom outlet of the dam if it can be seen, since the release for the fall is made through a valve there and not over the spillway; and the spillway itself in a wet spell, when the gates open automatically and the release becomes irrelevant.
The other end of the chain far down the same valley: the station's outfall back into the river, the switchyard, the line leaving the hill.
Instruments rather than people: gauge boards, staff gauges, a logged reading, a screen, a clock.
The roadside viewpoint itself, wide and from behind, as the place the schedule is actually addressed to - people arriving in daylight to look at a thing that is running because they will.
suggested_location.access: The fall is visible from the Hatton-Talawakele road with a short walk down towards the viewpoint, at about the 84 km post; one tourism listing says the viewpoint is maintained by the electricity authority and open from 08.30 to 17.30, which if correct sits inside the mandated sunrise-to-sunset release window and should be confirmed. The headworks sit on the same river just below Talawakele. Ground filming at the dam and any access to operating structures depends on the electricity authority, and the release itself is made through a valve at the dam's bottom outlet, so filming the cause rather than the effect means being admitted to the structure. Drone flight requires both defence clearance and civil aviation permission, and a dam, an underground power station and a switchyard are likely to fall inside restricted airspace: treat permission as genuinely uncertain and plan the film so that it works from the ground, with the aerial as a bonus rather than the spine. The two ground positions that carry it are the roadside viewpoint opposite the fall and the dry reach below the dam. The gorge itself is steep and wet and should not be entered for a shot.
suggested_location.best_time: This is the film's central production question and it has to be settled before travel. The fall runs on a daylight release fixed by regulation - a volume of 47,250 cubic metres within a window between sunrise and sunset - but the two readings of that condition in circulation describe different shooting days. If the flow is continuous for ten and a half hours, the film is one long run with a single start and a single end, and the shots to have are the first hour after the release begins, with low sun across the gorge so that falling water and dry rock are both legible, and the same frame again as the run ends. If instead the volume is delivered in ten half-hour periods, the same day contains ten starts and ten stops, the advancing tongue of water on dry rock can be filmed repeatedly, and the film should be built around repetition rather than a single arrival. Establish which it is, and the actual daily clock, with the operating authority before anything else. Beyond that: the drier months make the argument visible, because it is then that what falls is only what was let out; but the obligation appears to be conditional on the natural flow being there, so a hard dry spell can leave nothing to release and the fall a stain on the rock. The wet months undo the argument and are worth one visit for exactly that - the dam's spill gates open automatically in heavy rain over the catchment, three of them on the morning of 3 August 2026 and all five in a photograph of August 2012, and on those days the fall is briefly its old self and nobody is deciding anything. Shoot the aerial, if it is allowed, in raking early light; shoot the viewpoint when people are there, which is the same hours as the release.

suggested_location.research_note: Researched properly on 2026-09-26 and a historical_thread added. The single most important finding is that the release is a documented legal obligation and not a reported practice: the National Environmental (Upper Kotmale Hydro-Power Project - Monitoring) Regulations, No. 1 of 2003, published in Gazette Extraordinary No. 1283/19 of 10 April 2003 under section 32(2)(r) of the National Environmental Act No. 47 of 1980, fix the volume for this fall at 47,250 cubic metres within a sunrise-to-sunset window, and a 2006 MEng dissertation at the University of Moratuwa by R. A. L. Ranawake exists solely to automate the valve at the dam's bottom outlet that delivers it. What is NOT documented, and what the film turns on, is the shape of the daily schedule: nearly every secondary source says a continuous flow for 10 hours and 30 minutes daily, while the 2004 Environmental Foundation Limited paper, citing the gazette itself, says the same volume 'per day for ten half hour periods'. Those are different films and the gazette has to be read before a shooting plan is written; it was not read for this record. Two facts previously in this file are corrected. First, the diverted water does not go to another valley: the headrace tunnel runs down this same valley and the underground station at Niyamgamdora returns the water by a 0.46 km tailrace to the same river, about two kilometres above the confluence with the Puna Oya and about two kilometres above the older reservoir downstream - which is also why the connections entry separating this film from the drawdown film is now explicit rather than a note. Second, the closing beat's 'twenty minutes ago' has gone; no source documents the travel time from gate to lip. Figures kept as variants rather than averaged: dam height 34 m against 35.5 m, tunnel 12.5/12.8/12.89 km, turbines 2 x 75 MW against 2 x 77 MW, cost Rs. 37,269 million against Rs. 44 billion, households moved 470/495/524/538, EIA submitted September against December 1994, approval 1998 against 2000 against 2002, waterfalls affected five against six against seven, Yoxford alternative 100 MW against 120 MW. Note for the reader: this is the UPPER Kotmale structure at Talawakele, a small run-of-river pond of about 2.5 million cubic metres, and it is a different work from the large Kotmale reservoir downstream whose drawdown zone is taken elsewhere on the slate; the two must not be confused or filmed as a pair. The coordinates remain the published position of the fall, not of the dam, which sits upstream at approximately 6.9467, 80.6581, and both are desk figures. The one other waterfall found under a comparable written release obligation is Devon Falls, 18,000 cubic metres a day for a minimum of ten hours between sunrise and sunset, under the same regulation and with an express proviso that the water be available from the natural flow; Laxapana and Aberdeen Falls are reduced by diversion but no schedule was found for either. All seven images were confirmed to exist through the Commons query API and their camera dates read; the two pre-scheme photographs are captioned as predating the scheme, as required. Unverified and left as unknowns: whether the release is run to the regulation now, the travel time from gate to lip, whether the valve or the start of a run is visible at the dam, whether the official photographic record and flow gauging of the falls can be consulted, and whether any of this can be flown over.

unknowns: When the release actually runs, which is the central production fact and is not settled by anything found. The 2003 monitoring regulation fixes a volume and a daylight window, and two readings of the same condition are in circulation: a continuous flow for ten and a half hours between sunrise and sunset, and a total daily volume delivered in ten half-hour periods. A film built on the first would shoot one long run; a film built on the second would shoot ten starts and ten stops in a day. They are different films and the question has to be answered before a schedule is written.

Whether the release is run to the regulation now, by whom, and on what daily decision. The obligation is written as conditional on that quantity being available from the natural flow of the stream, so in a dry spell the schedule may be nominal, and travel accounts published since the scheme opened say the flow has dwindled badly. Only the operating authority and the monitoring committee can answer this.

The travel time between the gate and the lip of the fall, which is the interval the film is built on. Nothing found documents it, and the film should not put a number on it until somebody has timed it.

Whether the release valve's operation is visible or audible at the dam at all. The one engineering account found describes a dedicated valve near the bottom outlet, worked by a program with an operator's screen; whether any of that is filmable, and whether the start of a run shows at the structure or only downstream, is unknown.

Whether a gauge station on this fall can be seen or its readings obtained. Flow gauging of the affected falls and a standardised photographic record of them were both made conditions of the approval, which means an official series of photographs of this waterfall exists somewhere; whether it can be consulted is unknown.
Whether the electricity authority will allow filming at the headworks, and whether defence and civil aviation clearance for drone flight over a dam and a gorge is obtainable.
How much of the surrounding slope is planted estate, and whether the film can be framed to stay off it.
No operator, officer or resident has been found or approached. Everything here is a research direction.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. No location, scene or shot decisions are made at the idea stage.
